title: Typing React Props
summary: In TypeScript React projects, every component's props should have an explicit interface. Define an interface named after the component with Props suffix (e.g. MovieCardProps), then annotate the function parameter. TypeScript will error if a caller passes the wrong type, omits a required prop, or misspells a prop name. Optional props use ?. Children are typed as React.ReactNode. The convention is to destructure props inline and annotate the destructured parameter.
keyPoints: Define an interface for every component: interface MovieCardProps { title: string; rating: number }
Annotate the parameter: function MovieCard({ title, rating }: MovieCardProps)
Optional props: poster?: string — callers may omit it
Or use React.PropsWithChildren<MyProps> to add children to an existing interface
Avoid using React.FC<Props> — prefer plain function syntax with annotated parameter
TypeScript will catch missing props, wrong types, and extra unknown props at build time

exercises.prompt: Which correctly defines props and uses them in a MovieCard component?
options:
function MovieCard(title: string, rating: number) { return

{title}

}

interface MovieCardProps { title: string; rating: number } function MovieCard({ title, rating }: MovieCardProps) { return

{title}

}
exercises.answer:
interface MovieCardProps { title: string; rating: number } function MovieCard({ title, rating }: MovieCardProps) { return

{title}

}
exercises.explanation: Define the shape in a separate interface, then destructure and annotate the parameter. Listing props as individual function parameters does not work for React components.
value is required (no ?), max is optional. Omitting value errors. Passing value as a string '8.8' instead of a number 8.8 also errors — TypeScript checks the JSX attributes against the interface.

exercises.prompt:
How do you type a component that renders its children? function Card({ children }) { return
{children}
}
exercises.explanation: React.ReactNode accepts anything React can render: strings, numbers, JSX elements, arrays, null. JSX.Element only accepts JSX, which would reject strings and null as children.

exercises.prompt: You have MovieCardProps and want to add children without modifying the interface. Which utility type does this?
exercises.explanation: React.PropsWithChildren<T> is a built-in utility that adds children?: React.ReactNode to an existing props type. It lets you keep your interface clean and add children at the usage site.

exercises.prompt: Why is using React.FC<Props> discouraged in modern TypeScript React code?
options: React.FC does not support generic components
React.FC implicitly added children to props in older versions, hiding intent, and it is now an unnecessary wrapper
React.FC does not work with hooks
exercises.answer: React.FC implicitly added children to props in older versions, hiding intent, and it is now an unnecessary wrapper
exercises.explanation: Before React 18, React.FC automatically included children in every component's props, even when they shouldn't accept children. Modern practice is to use a plain function with an explicitly annotated parameter — it is simpler and clearer.
title and rating are required. poster is optional and can be omitted. Passing rating as the string '8.8' would error because the interface expects number.

exercises.prompt: Define a WatchButton component that accepts a required label (string) and an optional onWatch callback that takes no arguments and returns nothing:
exercises.explanation: Callback props are typed as function signatures. () => void means a function with no parameters that returns nothing. The ? makes it optional so the component can be used without passing a handler.
